capacityContract.purpose: The dispatch backpressure contract, defined once here so the Go, .NET, Python and Node drivers assert the same behaviour. Cases carrying "capacity": true need a negotiated window and several requests, so a generic per-case loop must skip them and drive them explicitly.
capacityContract.refusalScope: A case refuses only the connection's FIRST request id. "refusals" and "refuseAlways" describe what happens to that one request, not to every request on the connection: requests submitted behind it are always answered. The narrowing is deliberate and load-bearing -- it is what lets a case refuse one request and observe what the work queued behind it does (capacity-slot-order). Do not model "refusals": 1 as "the first attempt of every request is refused".
capacityContract.expectedSubmissions: Upper bound on the total number of application request frames the fixture expects on the connection, counting each resubmission under the same id as another submission. It is what separates paced resubmission from the hot retry loop the spec names an anti-goal, without asserting any duration: a client that resubmits instantly and forever blows through the bound long before any clock is consulted.
capacityContract.holdMs: How long the fixture holds the connection's first request before answering it (or, with "closeWhileParked", before closing the socket). Its presence is what makes a case a holding case. While the hold is active the fixture fails the case if a second frame arrives, so "the client parked rather than over-submitting" is proved by frame order rather than by timing.
capacityContract.waitingTimeoutMs: The per-request timeout a driver must give the request that parks behind the held one. It is deliberately much shorter than "holdMs": the request waits several times its own timeout for a slot, and the timeout must still be worth its full length from the moment the request is transmitted, because the deadline arms at transmit and never charges the wait.
capacityContract.silentAfterWait: The fixture answers the held request when its "holdMs" expires, and then never answers anything admitted afterwards. It is what makes the waiting request's own deadline the only thing that can settle it, so the case can tell "the deadline is in force from transmit, with the caller's own duration" apart from "no deadline was ever armed" and from "the request ran on the connection-level timeout". Without it the waiting request is answered in the same tick it is admitted and all three produce success, which is half the property.
capacityContract.waitingDelivery: The delivery code the waiting request must carry once its own deadline expires. The request was transmitted, so the work may have been done and the honest code is UNKNOWN (RESPONSE_LOST at the wire layer). A driver must also require the error to name a deadline, so a connection teardown cannot pass as an expiry.
capacityContract.waitingProbeMs: How long a driver may wait, measured from the window filling, for the waiting request to settle. It must sit well above "holdMs" + "waitingTimeoutMs" (when the correct deadline expires) and well below "holdMs" + the connection-level timeout (when a request wrongly running on the connection's deadline would expire). A request with no deadline at all never settles and is caught by the same probe. The slack above the correct expiry is scheduler tolerance; the slack below the wrong one is what keeps the case strict.
capacityContract.deliveryAlternates: Some capacity cases admit more than one honest delivery code, and a driver must accept any of them. capacity-refuse-always ends in a deadline expiry; the request is almost always inside a backoff pause when the deadline fires, which is NOT_SUBMITTED, but a deadline that lands in the sub-millisecond window between a transmit and the refusal arriving reports the wire code RESPONSE_LOST, which every SDK surfaces as the delivery UNKNOWN, and that is equally truthful. The invariant the case actually guarantees is a deadline expiry and never a CAPACITY_EXHAUSTED surfaced to the caller; pinning one delivery code makes the case flaky rather than strict. The alternate is tolerated ONLY for that sub-millisecond transmit/refusal race: NOT_SUBMITTED is the stronger claim and the one the spec says callers may act on, while UNKNOWN only says the server may have done work, so an SDK that ALWAYS reports the alternate is non-conforming even though this case accepts it. Absence of the field means the case admits exactly its "delivery" and nothing else; a driver must default it to the empty list rather than assume it is present. Every delivery value in this fixture is stated in SDK delivery vocabulary, never a wire code, so a driver compares it directly and never translates: this field once said RESPONSE_LOST, which no SDK ever reports as a delivery, so the tolerance was unreachable and the flake it existed to prevent was still live.
capacityContract.handshake: Refuses the "control" dispatch negotiation with CAPACITY_EXHAUSTED. A refused negotiation is never flow control and is never resubmitted: the server treats a second selection on one connection as a protocol violation. The harness asserts a negotiation was actually attempted and refused, so a language that never drives the case cannot report success.
